chapter_note.about: An ER diagram is a drawing of what a database must remember: the things (entities), their details (attributes) and how they connect (relationships). This chapter covers the kinds of attribute, cardinality and participation, weak entities, and the rules for turning a diagram into tables. It then covers the question GATE asks most, the minimum number of tables, followed by counting entities under constraints and reading a written specification into a diagram. Most questions come down to one habit: classify every piece of the diagram, then apply a fixed rule to it.
chapter_note.simple: Before building a shop's record system, you sketch what it must remember. Boxes are the things (customers, orders), ovals are details about a thing (name, phone), and diamonds say how two things are linked (a customer places orders). You also write how many on each side: one customer places many orders. Then the sketch is turned into tables using fixed rules: a plain detail becomes a column, a detail that can have several values gets its own table, and a many-to-many link gets its own table too. Counting tables is mostly counting boxes, lists, and many-to-many diamonds.

cards.title: Entity and attribute kinds
cards.simple: Imagine a school record for one patient or student. The roll number is like a name tag that no two people share: that is the key. The birthday is a plain single fact. The age is not stored at all, because you can work it out from the birthday whenever you need it. A person may have several allergies, so that detail is a list. An address is a bundle of smaller facts: city plus pin code. In exam words: attributes are key, simple, composite, multivalued or derived. A table gets one column per simple attribute and per component part, no column for derived ones, and a separate table for each multivalued one.
cards.idea: An **entity set** is a group of similar things, such as all patients, and each thing is described by **attributes**. There are five kinds: a **key** identifies one entity, a **simple** attribute holds one atomic value, a **composite** one is made of parts, a **multivalued** one holds several values, and a **derived** one is computed from another and not stored. Knowing the kind tells you exactly how it becomes a table.
cards.definition:
In an ER diagram:

- **Key:** oval with the name underlined. Unique per entity.
- **Simple:** plain oval, one atomic value.
- **Composite:** oval joined to ovals for its parts (address → city, zip).
- **Multivalued:** double oval. A set of values per entity.
- **Derived:** dashed oval. Computed from another attribute (age from dob).

A relational column holds one atomic value, so composite parts become separate columns, derived attributes disappear, and multivalued attributes move to their own table.
cards.intuition_full: The ER diagram is a drawing for people, so it allows things a table cannot hold: a list in one cell (multivalued), a bundle in one cell (composite), a number that is just a formula (derived). Each kind exists to keep the diagram honest about the real world. The table is a strict grid: one value per cell. The conversion rules are therefore forced. A bundle is split into its parts. A list needs a separate row for each value, so it needs its own table that points back to the owner by its key. A formula needs no storage because storing it would let it disagree with its source (age and dob could contradict). A key is the single most important attribute: if you cannot name it, you cannot build the table. A useful memory trick: ask of every oval, "how many values, and are they stored?" Many values: list table. Parts: columns. Computed: nothing.

examples.setup: Entity Patient has: pid (key), name, dob, age (derived from dob), allergies (multivalued), address (composite: city, zip). Classify each attribute and list the columns of the Patient table.
steps: Entity Patient has: pid, name, dob, age, allergies and address (with parts city and zip).
pid is the key: it becomes the primary key column.
name and dob are simple: one column each.
age is derived from dob: dashed oval, no column.

examples.setup: Instructor has: iid (key), name, email (multivalued), salary, join_year, experience (derived from join_year), office (composite: building, room). How many columns does the main Instructor table have, and how many tables are needed for this entity?

how: Circle each oval and name its kind: key, simple, composite, multivalued, derived.
Key and simple → a column each. Composite → one column per part.

cards.mistake: Counting a derived attribute as a column, or counting the composite oval together with its parts. The composite name is only a label; only its parts become columns. And never leave a multivalued attribute in a single cell.

A multivalued attribute that is also composite → its own table with one column per part.
Derived from another entity's data (e.g. number of orders) → still not stored.
A relation cannot hold a list in a cell, but an ER diagram can draw one.

cards.title: Relationships and cardinality
cards.simple: Think of customers and their orders. One customer can place many orders. But each single order belongs to just one customer. Read it from both sides: "from a customer, how many orders?" Many. "From an order, how many customers?" One. Two sides, two answers, and together they give the type of relationship. If both answers are "many", like students and clubs, it is many-to-many. In exam words: the cardinality ratio of a relationship is 1:1, 1:N or M:N. It is read by asking, for one entity on each side, how many entities of the other side it can be linked to.
cards.idea: A **relationship** links entity sets, drawn as a diamond. Its **cardinality ratio** says how many entities on one side can link to one entity on the other: 1:1, 1:N or M:N. To find it, pick one entity on each side in turn and count its partners. If every order has one customer but a customer has many orders, the ratio is 1:N from Customer to Order.
cards.definition:
For a relationship R between entity sets A and B:

- **1:1:** each A entity has at most one B partner, and each B entity has at most one A partner.
- **1:N** (one A, many B): each B has at most one A; an A may have many B.
- **M:N:** both sides may have many partners.
- The N sits next to the entity that can appear many times. The ratio is a rule of the situation (a constraint), not a fact about the rows that happen to exist.
cards.intuition_full: A ratio is two separate questions, and people mix them up by reading only one. Draw a dot for each entity of A on the left and each entity of B on the right, and a line for each relationship instance. Now look at the dots on the right: if every right dot has at most one line, then each B has one A; that gives the "1" on the A side. Then look at the left dots: if some have two lines, A may have many Bs; that gives the "N" on the B side. In a 1:N relationship the lines never merge on the many side. In an M:N relationship the picture is a tangle, and that tangle is exactly why it later needs its own table. A relationship is a rule about all possible data, so the ratio comes from the words of the specification ("each order has exactly one customer"), not from counting a few rows.

examples.setup: Customer places Order. Data: c1 placed o1, o2, o3; c2 placed o4; c3 placed o5, o6. What is the cardinality ratio?
steps: Two entity sets: Customer and Order.
A relationship Places connects them.
Expected ratio: 1 beside Customer and N beside Order. We check it against data.
Data: three customers c1, c2, c3 and six orders o1 to o6.
The lines: c1 placed o1, o2, o3; c2 placed o4; c3 placed o5, o6.
Order side: each of o1 to o6 has exactly one line, so one customer. Customer side: c1 has 3 lines, c3 has 2, c2 has 1, so many orders. That confirms 1:N from Customer to Order.
examples.answer: 1:N from Customer to Order (one customer, many orders).

examples.setup: Employee works-on Project. The relationship instances are (e1,p1), (e2,p1), (e2,p2), (e3,p2). What ratio do these data suggest, and why?
steps: Employees: e2 appears twice (p1 and p2). So one employee can have many projects.
Projects: p1 has e1 and e2; p2 has e2 and e3. So one project can have many employees.
Both sides have an entity with two partners.
examples.answer: M:N. The data show many on both sides. In an exam the specification wording decides, but data like this can only come from an M:N relationship.

examples.setup: Same Employee works-on Project, but the only instances stored so far are (e1,p1) and (e2,p2). The specification says "an employee can work on several projects and a project can have several employees". What is the ratio?
steps: The data alone look 1:1: every employee and every project appears once.
But cardinality is a constraint on all allowed data, so it comes from the rule in the specification.
The rule allows several partners on both sides.
examples.answer: M:N. A few rows do not prove a ratio; the specification does.

cards.title: Participation
cards.simple: Take the same shop. Every order must belong to a customer: an order without a customer makes no sense. But a customer may sign up and never buy anything. So the order side is "must" and the customer side is "may". Drawing a double line means "must take part": every single order has a customer. A single line means "may": some customers have no order. It is a rule about every entity of one side, not about the number of links. In exam words: total participation (double line) means every entity of the set appears in at least one relationship instance; partial participation (single line) means some may not.
cards.idea: **Participation** says whether an entity must take part in a relationship. **Total participation** (a double line) means every entity in the set is linked at least once. **Partial participation** (a single line) means some entities may be left out. It is separate from cardinality: cardinality counts how many partners, participation says whether there must be one at all.
cards.definition:
For entity set E and relationship R:

- **Total:** every $e\in E$ appears in at least one instance of R. Double line from E to R.
- **Partial:** some $e\in E$ may appear in no instance. Single line.
- With a 1:N relationship where the N side is total, every N entity has exactly one partner, so the number of R instances equals $|N\text{ side}|$.
- A weak entity always participates totally in its identifying relationship.
cards.intuition_full: Cardinality and participation answer different questions, and together they pin down the counting. Cardinality is about the maximum: "at most one customer per order". Participation is about the minimum: "at least one customer per order". Together, the order has exactly one customer. When the N side of a 1:N relationship is total, you can count instances by counting the N side only, since each N entity contributes exactly one instance. This is the source of the numeric traps in GATE: totality forces a lower bound on how many entities exist or are used. It also controls table design: if the N side is total, the foreign key column never holds NULL. If it were partial, some orders would have no customer and the foreign key could be NULL.

examples.setup: Department 1:N Course via Offers. Every course must be offered by a department, but a department may offer no course. There are 5 departments and 12 courses. How many instances does Offers have, and how many departments can be left with no course?
steps: Course is on the N side and total: each course has exactly one department.
So the number of instances = number of courses = 12.
Department is partial, so departments may be unused.
The 12 courses could all belong to one department. At least 1 department is used and up to 4 can be idle.
examples.answer: 12 instances. Between 0 and 4 departments can have no course (at least 1 department must be used).

examples.setup: Now Department is also total: every department must offer at least one course. There are 5 departments and 3 courses. Is this data possible?
steps: Each course has exactly one department (N side total, 1:N).
Each department needs at least one course (Department total).
5 departments need at least 5 different courses, because one course serves only one department.
There are only 3 courses.
examples.answer: Impossible. Total on the 1 side forces |Course| ≥ |Department|, and 3 < 5.

cards.title: Weak entities
cards.simple: Imagine rooms in different buildings. Building A has room 101 and Building B also has room 101. If someone says "room 101", you ask "in which building?" The room number alone does not tell you which room. A room can only be pointed at together with its building. A thing like this, which cannot be identified on its own, is called weak. It borrows part of its identity from its owner. In exam words: a weak entity set has no key of its own; it has a partial key (discriminator). Its key is the owner's key plus the partial key. It is drawn as a double rectangle, tied to the owner by a double diamond, with total participation.
cards.idea: A **weak entity** cannot be told apart without its owner. Rooms are numbered 101, 102 in every building, so a room number alone does not identify a room. The weak entity has a **partial key** (here rno) that only distinguishes rooms inside one building. Its full key is the **owner's key plus the partial key**: (bname, rno). It is drawn as a double rectangle linked to its owner by a double diamond.
cards.definition:
- **Owner (strong) entity:** has a key of its own.
- **Weak entity set W:** no key of its own; has a **partial key** (discriminator), underlined with a dashed line.
- **Identifying relationship:** double diamond from owner to W. W has **total** participation (double line), and the relationship is 1:N from owner to W.
- **Key of W** $=$ key of owner $\cup$ partial key of W.
- In the relational model W becomes one table; the identifying relationship adds no table.
cards.intuition_full: Why not just give the weak entity its own key? Because in the real situation it has none: room numbers genuinely repeat across buildings. We could add an artificial id, but the model wants to show that the room exists only because of the building. If the building is deleted, its rooms go with it. That dependency is what the double diamond and the total participation express. In the table, the owner key becomes a foreign key inside the weak table, and it is part of the primary key. So the weak table's key has the owner's key columns first and the partial key after. A weak entity can itself own another weak entity, and then the keys accumulate.

examples.setup: Building (key bname) owns Room (partial key rno). Rooms: (A,101), (A,102), (B,101). Why is Room weak, and what is its table key?
steps: Building is a strong entity with key bname.

So Room is a weak entity: a double rectangle tied to its owner Building by a double diamond, with total participation.
rno is only a partial key, the discriminator inside one building. It is underlined with a dashed line.
Key of the Room table = owner key + partial key = (bname, rno): (A,101), (A,102), (B,101) are all different.
examples.answer: Room is weak. Its table is Room(bname, rno, ...) with PRIMARY KEY (bname, rno).

Add the owner's key lno as a foreign key (and part of the key): columns lno, payno, amount, date = 4.
Primary key = owner key + partial key = (lno, payno).
The identifying relationship adds no table; Loan and Payment are the only two tables.
examples.answer: Payment(lno, payno, amount, date), key (lno, payno): 4 attributes. 2 tables for Loan and Payment.

cards.title: Entities to tables
cards.simple: A table is a strict grid: one value in each box. So a drawing with lists and bundles must be converted. A plain detail gets a column. A bundle, like a director with first and last name, is opened up into its parts, one column each. A detail that can be worked out, like age, is skipped. A detail that can have a list, like genres, cannot fit in one box, so it gets its own small table: movie id and one genre per row. In exam words: map each entity set to a table with its key as the primary key; flatten composite attributes, drop derived ones, and make a new table (owner key, value) for each multivalued attribute whose key is the pair.
cards.idea: Every entity set becomes a **table** with its key as the primary key. Simple attributes become columns. A composite attribute becomes one column per part. A derived attribute gets no column. A multivalued attribute becomes a **separate table** with columns (owner key, value), and the primary key is both columns together.
cards.definition:
For an entity E with key $k$:

- Table $E(k,\ \text{simple attributes},\ \text{parts of composites})$.
- Derived attributes: omitted.
- For each multivalued attribute $m$: table $E\_m(k,\ m)$ with primary key $(k,m)$ and $k$ a foreign key to $E$.
- Number of tables for E $=1+$ number of multivalued attributes.
cards.intuition_full: The conversion rules follow from one demand: every cell holds one atomic value, and no value is stored twice. A composite attribute is split because a cell cannot hold a bundle, and its parts are exactly the atomic values. A derived attribute is dropped because storing it would duplicate information and risk disagreement. A multivalued attribute is the interesting case: if you put m1's genres in one cell as "drama, comedy", you lose the ability to search a single genre or to enforce a rule on each one. A separate table with one row per (movie, genre) pair fixes this. Its primary key is both columns because the same movie appears in many rows and the same genre appears for many movies; only the pair is unique. The key k in the new table is a foreign key that keeps each genre attached to a real movie.

examples.setup: Entity Movie: mid (key), title, year, age (derived), genres (multivalued), director (composite: dir_fname, dir_lname). Write the tables.

Composite director → two columns dir_fname, dir_lname. The main table so far has 5 columns.
Derived age → no column.
Multivalued genres → new table MovieGenre(mid, genre). Rows like (m1, drama), (m1, comedy).
Primary key of MovieGenre is (mid, genre); mid is a foreign key to Movie.
examples.answer: Movie(mid, title, year, dir_fname, dir_lname) and MovieGenre(mid, genre). Two tables, 5 + 2 columns.

examples.setup: Entity Course: cid (key), title, credits, prereq (multivalued), schedule (composite: day, slot). Count the tables and the total number of columns over all tables.

Tables: 1 + 1 = 2. Columns: 5 + 2 = 7.

cards.title: Relationships to tables
cards.simple: When one customer has many orders, each order card just writes down "my customer is c1". One extra box in the order card is enough, and that is called a foreign key. But when many actors are in many movies, an actor card cannot hold a list of movies, and a movie card cannot hold a list of actors. You need a separate sheet where each line says "this actor in this movie". That sheet is the table for the many-to-many relationship. In exam words: for a 1:N relationship, put the key of the 1 side into the N side's table as a foreign key; for M:N, create a new table with both keys (together the primary key) plus any relationship attributes.
cards.idea: How a relationship becomes tables depends on its ratio. For **1:N**, add the key of the 1 side to the N side's table as a **foreign key**: no new table. For **1:1**, put the key on either side, best on the side with total participation. For **M:N**, create a **new table** holding both keys plus any attributes of the relationship; the pair of keys is its primary key.
cards.definition:
For a relationship R between A (key $a$) and B (key $b$):

- **1:N** (A is the 1 side): add $a$ to table B as a foreign key. Relationship attributes also go into B.
- **1:1:** add the key of one side to the other, preferably to the side with total participation (so no NULLs).
- **M:N:** table $R(a,\ b,\ \text{attrs})$, primary key $(a,b)$, with foreign keys to A and B.
- **n-ary:** a table with the key of every participating entity.
cards.intuition_full: The rule is about where information can live without repeating or leaving gaps. In a 1:N relationship, each N entity has exactly one partner, so a single column on the N side records it fully. Putting the foreign key on the 1 side instead would need a list per cell, which a table cannot hold. In an M:N relationship neither side has a single partner, so no column in either table can store the link; the link itself must become rows. The new table has one row per relationship instance, which is why its natural primary key is the pair of keys: the same pair cannot occur twice. In a 1:1 relationship either side works, but the side with total participation is better because the foreign key is never NULL. A relationship attribute such as role belongs wherever its owning link lives: in the link table for M:N, or in the N side for 1:N.

cards.title: Count minimum tables
cards.simple: Counting the tables is like counting the files you need in a cabinet. Every box (entity) needs one file. Every list inside a box (multivalued attribute) needs one more file. Every many-to-many link needs one more file. A one-to-many link needs no new file: it is just an extra line in an existing file. So you count boxes, lists and many-to-many links, and ignore the rest. In exam words: minimum tables = entity sets + multivalued attributes + M:N relationships + n-ary relationships. 1:N and 1:1 relationships fold into an existing table.
cards.idea: To find the **minimum number of tables** for an ER diagram, count: one per **entity set**, one per **multivalued attribute**, one per **M:N relationship**, and one per **n-ary** (three or more entities) relationship. A 1:N or 1:1 relationship adds nothing, because it folds into a table that already exists as a foreign key.
cards.definition:
$\text{tables}=\#\text{entity sets}+\#\text{multivalued attributes}+\#\text{M:N relationships}+\#\text{n-ary relationships}$

- Weak entities count as entity sets; their identifying relationship adds nothing.
- 1:N and 1:1 relationships add **0**.
- If two entities are joined by a 1:1 relationship with **total** participation on both sides, they can be merged into one table, so the count drops by 1.
cards.intuition_full: The formula follows directly from the conversion rules. Every piece of the diagram either needs a table of its own or can be stored inside another table. An entity is stored as its own table. A multivalued attribute needs a table because a cell cannot hold a list. A many-to-many relationship needs a table because neither side can hold a list of partners. A ternary relationship needs a table for the same reason. A 1:N relationship needs nothing, because the N side can hold one foreign key per row. This also explains why "minimum" is in the question: you could give a 1:N relationship its own table, but you are not forced to, and minimum means we avoid that waste. The one case that reduces the count further is the 1:1 relationship with total participation on both sides: every A has a B and every B has an A, so a single combined table has no NULLs.

Multivalued attribute allergies = 1 table (Allergy).
M:N relationship Treats = 1 table.
1:N relationship In = 0 tables (a wid foreign key goes into Patient).
examples.answer: 5 tables: Doctor, Patient, Ward, Allergy, Treats.

cards.what_full:
To find the **minimum number of tables** for an ER diagram, count: one per **entity set**, one per **multivalued attribute**, one per **M:N relationship**, and one per **n-ary** (three or more entities) relationship. A 1:N or 1:1 relationship adds nothing, because it folds into a table that already exists as a foreign key.

$\text{tables}=\#\text{entity sets}+\#\text{multivalued attributes}+\#\text{M:N relationships}+\#\text{n-ary relationships}$

- Weak entities count as entity sets; their identifying relationship adds nothing.
- 1:N and 1:1 relationships add **0**.
- If two entities are joined by a 1:1 relationship with **total** participation on both sides, they can be merged into one table, so the count drops by 1.

2. Multivalued attribute allergies = 1 table (Allergy).
3. M:N relationship Treats = 1 table.
4. 1:N relationship In = 0 tables (a wid foreign key goes into Patient).

cards.title: Counting under constraints
cards.simple: Suppose 9 students must each pick one of 4 clubs. However you spread them, some club gets at least 3 students, because 4 clubs with only 2 each hold just 8. That is the pigeonhole idea: more pigeons than holes means some hole is crowded. An ER diagram can say the same thing. If every entity on the left must link to exactly one entity on the right, then the left entities are the pigeons and the right entities are the holes. In exam words: use cardinality and participation to count the relationship instances, and use the pigeonhole principle to bound how many partners some entity must have.
cards.idea: Cardinality and participation turn into numbers. A **many-to-one** relationship with **total** participation on the many side gives exactly one instance per entity on that side. With $n$ such entities and $m$ entities on the other side, the pigeonhole principle forces some entity to have at least $\lceil n/m\rceil$ partners. Totality on the other side gives a lower bound on how many entities are used.
cards.definition:
Let R be many-to-one from E1 to E2.

- If E1 is **total**: instances $=|E_1|$. Some E2 entity has at least $\lceil |E_1|/|E_2|\rceil$ partners.
- If E1 is **partial**: instances $\le |E_1|$.
- If E2 is **total** (every E2 has a partner): instances $\ge |E_2|$, and in particular $|E_1|\ge|E_2|$ when each E1 has at most one partner.
- Always: instances $\le |E_1|$ for a many-to-one R.
cards.intuition_full: There are only two kinds of reasoning here. First, a counting argument: each line of the relationship is an edge from an E1 entity to an E2 entity; at most one edge leaves each E1 entity (many-to-one), and total participation says at least one does. That is exactly one edge per E1 entity, so the number of edges is |E1|. Second, the pigeonhole principle: spread n edges over m E2 entities; if every E2 entity had at most k partners, there could be at most m·k edges. So n ≤ m·k, and k ≥ n/m. Since k is a whole number, round up. For lower bounds with totality on E2, each E2 entity needs its own edge, and edges from E1 entities are all distinct (each E1 has at most one edge), so you need at least |E2| edges. Draw the two columns of dots and the argument becomes almost obvious.

examples.setup: R is many-to-one from E1 to E2 with total participation on E1. |E1| = 9 and |E2| = 4. How many instances does R have, and what is the smallest possible maximum number of partners of one E2 entity?
steps: E1 has 9 entities and E2 has 4. R is many-to-one from E1, total on E1: each E1 entity has exactly one partner, so R has 9 instances.
Spread the lines as evenly as possible: the first 4 lines give f1 two partners and f2 two partners.
The next 4 lines give f3 two and f4 two: 8 lines used, perfectly even.
The 9th line must land on some E2 entity, which then has 3 partners.
No arrangement does better: ⌈9/4⌉ = 3.
examples.answer: 9 instances. At least one E2 entity has 3 or more partners (⌈9/4⌉ = 3).

examples.setup: R is many-to-one from E1 to E2 (each E1 entity has at most one partner). E2 participates totally: every E2 entity has at least one partner. |E1| = 10, |E2| = 7. What is the minimum and maximum number of instances of R?
steps: Each E1 entity gives at most one instance, so instances ≤ 10.
Each E2 entity needs at least one partner, and no E1 entity is shared between two E2 entities (one partner each).
So at least 7 different E1 entities are used: instances ≥ 7.
Both bounds can be reached: 7 E1 entities linked one-to-one, or all 10 linked.
examples.answer: Minimum 7, maximum 10.

examples.setup: Same R, but now E1 is total (every E1 entity has exactly one partner) instead of E2. |E1| = 10, |E2| = 7. How many instances?
steps: Total on E1 with many-to-one: exactly one instance per E1 entity.
So instances = 10, exactly.
E2 is now partial, so some E2 entities may have no partner.
examples.answer: 10 instances, no range. Totality on the many side pins the count exactly.

If |E1| ≤ |E2| the pigeonhole bound is just 1.

cards.title: Spec to diagram
cards.simple: A written description of a system hides a diagram inside it. Read it once and mark three kinds of words. The naming words (member, book, publisher) are the boxes. The doing words (borrow, publishes) are the links between boxes. The counting words (a member can borrow many books, each book has one publisher) say what the numbers on the links are. A detail that belongs to the link itself, like the date a book was borrowed, hangs off the link. Boxes never connect directly: there is always a diamond in between. In exam words: nouns become entities, verbs become relationships, quantifiers give cardinality, and entities connect only through relationship diamonds.
cards.idea: To draw an ER diagram from a specification, read it once and mark three things. **Nouns** are entity candidates. **Verbs** are relationships. Words such as "each", "many", "exactly one" give **cardinality and participation**. Attributes hang off entities, or off a relationship if they describe the link itself. Entities never connect directly; they are joined through a relationship diamond.
cards.definition:
Procedure:

1. List the nouns. Those with attributes of their own become entity sets.
2. List the verbs that link two nouns. Each becomes a relationship.
3. Quantifiers decide the ratio: "a member may borrow many books" and "a book may be borrowed by many members" give M:N.
4. A fact that depends on the pair (e.g. date of loan) is an attribute of the relationship.
5. A thing that needs another to exist or be numbered within it is a weak entity.
cards.intuition_full: Writing English into a diagram is a translation exercise with a small dictionary. Nouns that have details or that can be counted become boxes. Verbs that connect two such boxes become diamonds. The quantifier words give the numbers, and you must read each quantifier from both sides, because a sentence about members borrowing books says nothing yet about books being borrowed by members unless the text states it. Pay special attention to the attribute-or-entity decision: a noun with its own attributes or its own relationships should be an entity; a plain description should be an attribute. And be careful about where a detail belongs. A date of borrowing belongs to neither the member nor the book, only to the pair, so it hangs from the relationship diamond. This will matter when you count tables: it makes the Borrows table need a date column.

examples.setup: A library keeps Members, Books and Publishers. A member can borrow many books, and a book can be borrowed by many members; each loan has a date. Each book has one publisher, and a publisher publishes many books. Draw the diagram and count the minimum tables.
steps: Read the specification once. Nouns are entity candidates, verbs are relationships, quantifiers give cardinality.
Nouns with their own identity: Member, Book, Publisher → three entity sets.
"borrow" links Member and Book. Many on both sides → M:N relationship Borrows. The date describes the loan, so it is an attribute of Borrows.
"publishes" links Publisher and Book. One publisher, many books → 1:N (1 at Publisher, N at Book).
Tables: Member, Book, Publisher = 3, plus Borrows (M:N) = 4. The 1:N Publishes folds into Book as a publisher key.
examples.answer: Diagram: Member -M:N (Borrows, date)- Book -N:1- Publisher. Minimum 4 tables.

examples.setup: A school has Classes and Teachers. Within each class the sections are numbered 1, 2, 3, and a section cannot exist without its class. Each section is taught by exactly one teacher, and a teacher teaches many sections. How many tables, and what is the key of the section table?
steps: Entities: Class, Teacher, Section.
"numbered within each class, cannot exist without its class": Section is a weak entity of Class, with partial key secno.
"taught by exactly one teacher; a teacher teaches many sections": 1:N from Teacher to Section, with Section total.
Tables: Class, Teacher, Section = 3. Both relationships fold: Section carries the class key and the teacher key.
Key of Section = (cid, secno); tid is a foreign key.
examples.answer: 3 tables. Section(cid, secno, tid) with primary key (cid, secno).

examples.setup: Each employee has a department. A department has a name, a budget and a manager. Should "department" be an attribute of Employee or an entity set?
steps: An attribute is a plain description with no structure of its own.
Department has its own attributes (name, budget) and its own relationships (it has a manager, it has many employees).
Storing it inside Employee would repeat the same name and budget on every employee row.
examples.answer: Make Department an entity set linked to Employee by a 1:N relationship. A noun with its own attributes or relationships is an entity.

scenes.title: The five kinds of attribute on one entity

objects.text:
Patient table:
pid name dob
city zip
(no age column)

Allergy table:
pid allergy

steps.caption: Patient is an entity set. Each oval hangs off it as an attribute. We classify the six attributes by kind.
**Key** attribute: pid identifies a patient. It is underlined. Its values never repeat.
**Simple** attributes: name and dob each hold one atomic value.
**Derived** attribute: age is computed from dob, so it is drawn dashed and will not be stored as a column.
**Multivalued** attribute: a patient can have several allergies. It is drawn with a double outline.
**Composite** attribute: address is made of parts, city and zip. Each part will become its own column.
Result: the Patient table has 5 columns (pid, name, dob, city, zip). age is dropped, and allergies move to a separate Allergy(pid, allergy) table.

scenes.title: One customer, many orders: read the ratio from instances

steps.caption: Two entity sets: Customer and Order.
A relationship Places connects them: a customer places orders.
Customer side is 1 (an order has exactly one customer). Order side is N (a customer may have many orders). This is a 1:N relationship from Customer to Order.
Now look at real data. Three customers and six orders.
Each line is one "places" instance: c1 placed o1, o2, o3; c2 placed o4; c3 placed o5, o6.
Check from the order side: pick o4. It has exactly one line, so one customer. Check from the customer side: c1 has three lines, so many orders. That confirms 1:N.

scenes.title: Total participation: every order must have a customer

steps.caption: The same Customer 1:N Order relationship. Now we also record participation: must every entity take part?
A **double line** on the Order side means total participation: every order must be placed by some customer.
A **single line** on the Customer side means partial participation: a customer may exist without ever placing an order.
Instances: four customers, five orders, and the "places" lines.
Total side check: every order node has a line. If one order had no line, the data would break the rule.
Partial side check: customer c4 has no line. This is allowed. Only if Customer were total would c4 be illegal.

scenes.title: A weak entity borrows its key from its owner

steps.caption: Building is a normal (strong) entity. Its key bname is underlined.
Rooms are numbered 101, 102 inside each building. Building A and Building B both have a room 101, so rno alone cannot identify a room.
Room is therefore a weak entity: a double rectangle. It is tied to its owner Building by an identifying relationship, a double diamond, with a double line (total participation).
rno is only a partial key, a discriminator. It tells rooms apart inside one building, so it is underlined with a dashed line.
The Room table key = owner key + partial key = (bname, rno). Now (A,101) and (B,101) are different rows.
Entity Movie with a key (mid), simple attributes, one derived attribute (age), one multivalued (genres) and one composite (director with fname, lname).
Main table Movie: the key mid becomes the primary key, and each simple attribute becomes a column: mid, title, year.
Composite director is flattened: one column per part, dir_fname and dir_lname. The Movie table now has 5 columns.
Derived age is not stored. It can be computed from year, so it gets no column.
Multivalued genres cannot sit in one cell. It gets its own table MovieGenre(mid, genre). Its primary key is both columns together, since one movie has many genres.

scenes.title: Foreign key for 1:N, a new table for M:N

steps.caption: 1:N relationship: one customer places many orders. We have two tables, Customer and Order.
Put the key of the 1 side into the N side as a foreign key. Order gets a cid column, and every order points to exactly one customer.

set.text: foreign key on the N side

steps.caption: M:N relationship: an actor acts in many movies and a movie has many actors. A single foreign-key column would need several values in one cell, which a table cannot hold.
Make a new table Acts. It holds both keys and the relationship attribute role. Each row is one fact: this actor in this movie.
The primary key of Acts is the pair (aid, mid): one row per actor-movie pair. Each column also stays a foreign key back to its parent.

scenes.title: Counting the minimum number of tables

steps.caption: ER diagram: Doctor M:N Patient (Treats), Ward 1:N Patient (In), and Patient has a multivalued attribute allergies.
Rule 1: every entity set needs a table. Doctor, Patient, Ward: 3 tables.
Rule 2: every multivalued attribute needs a table. allergies gives Allergy(pid, allergy): 4 tables.
Rule 3: every M:N relationship needs a table. Treats gives Treats(did, pid): 5 tables.
The 1:N relationship In costs nothing. Its key (wid) is added to Patient as a foreign key. No new table. Minimum number of tables = 5.

objects.text: R: many-to-one from E1 (9) to E2 (4); E1 is total

steps.caption: Each E1 entity relates to exactly one E2 entity (many-to-one, total on E1). So every one of the 9 E1 entities needs one line to some E2 entity. Counters show how many E1 partners each E2 entity has.
Start spreading the lines as evenly as possible: e1, e2 go to f1; e3, e4 go to f2.
e5, e6 go to f3; e7, e8 go to f4. Every E2 entity now has 2 partners: 8 lines used, perfectly even.
e9 must also draw one line, and every f already has 2. Whichever f it picks, that f reaches 3 partners.
So at least one E2 entity has 3 or more partners, because ⌈9/4⌉ = 3. Also, the number of R instances is exactly 9 (one per E1 entity). Some E2 entities could have none.

set.text: at least ⌈9/4⌉ = 3 partners; R has 9 instances

scenes.title: Reading a specification into an ER diagram

objects.text: 1. A library keeps Members, Books and Publishers.

2. A member can borrow many books, and a book can be
    borrowed by many members. Each loan has a date.

3. Each book has one publisher; a publisher
    publishes many books.

steps.caption: Read the specification once. Nouns are entity candidates, verbs are relationships, and phrases like "many" give the cardinality.
Sentence 1 names three nouns: Member, Book, Publisher. Draw them as entity rectangles.
Sentence 2: "borrow" is a relationship. Many members borrow many books, so it is M:N. The "date" belongs to the loan, not to either entity, so it hangs off the diamond.
Sentence 3: "has / publishes" is a relationship. One publisher, many books: 1 on the Publisher side, N on the Book side.
Count the tables: Member, Book (with a publisher foreign key), Publisher, and Borrows(mid, bid, date) for the M:N link. The 1:N Publishes adds no table.
